No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence yet about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion matters. 2. config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components) is the simplest configuration in the space. It sets a reference baseline, so later experiments can each change one factor and be compared against it: RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), modality (image-only, multimodal), or profile setting and aggregation (multiprofile with avgpool or transformer). 3. Under a limited budget, an interpretable baseline is the most useful first experiment. It lets us measure whether added complexity actually improves accuracy, rather than assuming it does, and it avoids starting with a configuration that changes many design choices at once.

1. Evidence and uncertainty: The only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). We have no information on whether the imaging modality carries useful signal, and most of the remaining search space (36 of 50 configurations) is multimodal. 2. What this tests: The image-only, single-profile ResNet50 configuration keeps the profile setting fixed and uses no aggregation or fusion. This gives a clean unimodal image baseline to compare directly against the RNA baseline. 3. Why it is the best next use of budget: Whether images are weaker than, comparable to, or stronger than RNA largely decides how much of the remaining budget should go to multimodal fusion versus RNA encoder and profile-setting variants. Running this before any multimodal or multiprofile experiment avoids changing several design choices at once and makes later multimodal results interpretable.

1. Evidence so far: RNA-only with PCA (config_001, acc 0.485, F1 0.464) clearly beats image-only with ResNet50 (config_010, acc 0.208, F1 0.172). RNA looks like the stronger modality. However, we have only these two runs, and the profile setting is still completely unexplored. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the best-known setup (RNA-only, PCA) and changes one thing, switching from single-profile to multi-profile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling several profiles helps. 3. Why it is the best next run: profile setting is a structural choice that affects about two-thirds of the remaining search space, so its answer guides most later decisions. Starting from the strong RNA baseline gives a clean, high-signal comparison. Avgpool is the cheapest, lowest-variance test, and comparisons of transformer aggregation, other encoders, or multimodal fusion can follow.

1. Evidence: RNA is clearly the stronger modality so far (0.485 vs 0.208 accuracy for image-only). Moving the PCA RNA model from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool gave a large gain (0.485 to 0.591 accuracy; F1 0.464 to 0.573). Multiprofile is therefore the most promising direction. We do not yet know whether the aggregation method matters. 2. This experiment keeps the best configuration fixed (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000) and changes only avgpool to transformer. That isolates the effect of aggregation and shows whether a learned, attention-based summary across profiles adds value beyond simple averaging. 3. It builds directly on the strongest result with a single-variable change, so it tests a likely improvement while also answering a design question. The answer shapes many later choices, because aggregation appears in most of the remaining multiprofile and multimodal configurations. Testing multimodal fusion or other RNA encoders before settling this would leave a key, widely shared factor unresolved.

Test: config_037 is identical to config_025 except that the RNA encoder is scVI instead of PCA. It is also config_005 with ViT-L image features added through weighted fusion. Why now: It exploits the best-supported settings for representation, profile setting, aggregation and fusion while changing only one factor relative to two existing runs. Either outcome is informative and directly guides the remaining budget, and it is the most likely candidate for a new best.

Either outcome reduces uncertainty on the design choice with the least evidence, and it does so more efficiently than re-testing fusion or encoders, which already have clearer support.

1. Evidence: we have only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI, ResNet50, avgpool and weighted fusion (config_016) reached 0.678 accuracy and 0.646 F1 at 5.9 GPU hours. 1) Evidence: scVI RNA with the ViT-L image encoder is clearly the strongest combination so far. config_033 (transformer, weighted) leads at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1, and config_027 (transformer, concat) is close behind at 0.721. The concat-versus-weighted fusion question can follow on the winning encoder. 1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 reached 0.706 to 0.715 accuracy, while pca_n2000 reached about 0.635 to 0.639 and scgpt reached 0.542. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.706 and 0.715, versus 0.635 to 0.639 for pca and 0.542 for scgpt). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 with scvi (0.715 vs 0.632). 1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT (0.706–0.715 vs ≤0.639). ViT-L also clearly beats ResNet50 when paired with scVI (0.715 vs 0.632). 1) Evidence: scVI-200 RNA plus ViT-L images, multiprofile, is clearly the strongest region, at 0.706–0.721. Swapping in ResNet50, PCA or scGPT drops accuracy sharply. The best result so far is config_034 (transformer, concat) at 0.7207. 1) Evidence: no experiments have been completed, so every design choice is uncertain. 1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_004 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, avgpool, concat) reached 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1 for 4.49 GPU hours. 1. Evidence so far: the two runs share scvi_n200, ViT-L and concat fusion and differ only in aggregation. 1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. Swapping scvi_n200 for scgpt dropped accuracy from about 0.72 to 0.51. 1. Evidence: The RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. scvi_n200 reaches about 0.715 to 0.721 accuracy, far above pca_n2000 (0.599) and scgpt (0.507). 1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder so far, at about 0.715-0.725 accuracy versus 0.60 for PCA and 0.51 for scGPT. Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion each gave small gains, and the current best is config_050 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725 accuracy. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (~0.72 versus 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt). ImageNet ViT-L slightly beats ResNet50 on accuracy (0.725 vs 0.713) and trained cheaper here (3.60 vs 6.22 GPU h). Weighted fusion edged out concat with transformer aggregation (0.725 vs 0.721). 1) Evidence: the scVI RNA encoder is clearly the most important choice so far (about 0.71-0.725, versus 0.60 for PCA and 0.51 for scGPT). Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor. With the same multiprofile ViT-L transformer setup, scvi_n200 scored about 0.72, pca_n2000 0.60 and scgpt 0.51. Evidence: every top result (0.706-0.725) uses scVI RNA with multiprofile multimodal input. The best is config_050 (ViT-L, transformer, weighted, 0.725). scGPT (0.507) and PCA (0.599) RNA encoders, single-profile input (0.537) and RNA-only (0.653) are all clearly worse. 1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so I am relying on priors. In multimodal cellular profiling, combining RNA and image features and aggregating across multiple profiles usually beats single-modality or single-profile setups. A learned transformer aggregator and a strong pretrained image encoder (ViT-L) are plausible accuracy gains, and scVI is a compact, well-regarded RNA representation. 2. What this tests: config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) is my best guess at a near-top configuration. It sets a high-performing anchor early. Later experiments can then run cheaper one-factor ablations against it: avgpool instead of transformer, ResNet50 instead of ViT-L, single-profile, unimodal baselines, and weighted fusion or other RNA encoders. These will show which expensive components actually pay off. 3. Why now: Only the best accuracy counts, so securing a strong result first reduces risk, and every later comparison becomes informative relative to this anchor. Expected cost is high relative to the pool, since multiprofile transformer aggregation, multimodal processing and large ViT-L representations all add cost. I accept that cost once because this configuration is the most likely to be top-performing, and I plan to use cheaper variants for the following experiments.

1) Evidence: only one result exists. config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1 at 4.65 GPU hours. If avgpool matches or beats the transformer, many cheaper configurations become attractive. Evidence: the two completed runs share scvi_n200, ViT-L, multiprofile and concat fusion, and differ only in aggregation. 1) Evidence: with scVI RNA and concat fusion, ViT-L clearly beat ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688 with transformer aggregation). 1) Evidence: scVI-n200 with ViT-L is the strongest combination so far (0.721 with transformer, 0.715 with avgpool). ViT-L beats ResNet50 by about 3 points, and scGPT performs far worse (0.507). 1. Evidence: scVI RNA with the ImageNet ViT-L image encoder is clearly the strongest combination. 1) Evidence: all four scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l multiprofile combinations have now been tested. They sit in a narrow band of 0.706–0.725. 1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy. scvi_n200 clearly beats the other RNA encoders (pca 0.586, scGPT 0.507). 1) Evidence: In the two experiments so far, only the image encoder changed. Swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l raised validation accuracy from 0.688 to 0.721 and F1 from 0.659 to 0.681, and the ViT-L run was slightly cheaper (4.65 vs 5.16 GPU hours). The prior that this region is strong comes from general expectations (combining modalities and aggregating profiles often helps), not from data in this study. The result will give a reference accuracy for later one-factor comparisons: transformer vs avgpool, ViT-L vs ResNet50, weighted vs concat fusion, and multimodal vs unimodal ablations. 3) Why now: It probably captures most of the benefit of the expensive variants at a fraction of their cost. That keeps total GPU hours low while giving a solid baseline that the remaining 9 experiments can refine. Expected relative cost: moderate. It is above single-profile and unimodal configs because of multiprofile and multimodal processing, but below configs using transformer aggregation or ViT-L.

1) Evidence so far: there is a single result. The multimodal, multiprofile model with scVI-200, ResNet50, avgpool aggregation and concat fusion (config_031) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1, so we have a baseline but no comparisons yet. 2) What this tests: config_010 changes only the aggregation, from avgpool to a learned transformer, and keeps everything else fixed. Any difference can therefore be attributed to aggregation. That clarifies a design choice that applies to every multiprofile configuration, which is most of the search space. A learned aggregator over multiple profiles is a plausible source of accuracy gains over simple mean pooling. 3) Why now: a clean one-factor comparison against the only baseline gives the most decision-relevant information for planning the remaining 8 experiments. It does this without jumping to the much costlier ViT-L encoder. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_031, perhaps around 8–10 GPU hours, because of transformer aggregation over profiles. It should still be well below the cost of ViT-L configurations.

1) Evidence: the two runs differ only in aggregation. Transformer aggregation (config_010) reached 0.688 accuracy and 0.659 F1, versus 0.632 and 0.607 for avgpool (config_031). It also trained faster (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU hours). This is a single comparison, but the gap of about 5.6 points is consistent across both metrics, so the transformer configuration is a reasonable base to build on. The image encoder, RNA encoder and fusion type are all still untested. 2) Test: config_029 keeps the best setup (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, transformer, concat) and changes only the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l. This isolates whether a larger pretrained vision backbone improves accuracy. 3) Why now: the image representation is plausibly the factor with the largest remaining effect on accuracy. Answering it early tells me which image encoder to use when I later vary the RNA encoder and fusion type. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_010, roughly 6-9 GPU hours, because ViT-L produces larger representations. That cost is justified because this run could set a new best and shapes the rest of the search.

1) Evidence so far: transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool with ResNet50 (0.688 vs 0.632). Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L then raised accuracy further to 0.721, with F1 also up to 0.681. That makes config_029 (scvi_n200, ViT-L, transformer, concat) the current best. Fusion has never been varied: all three runs used concat. The RNA encoder also remains untested. 2) This experiment changes only the fusion method to weighted on the best configuration. It isolates whether weighted fusion improves on concat in the strongest setting found so far. 3) It is a direct exploit of the leading direction and also reduces uncertainty on an unexplored design axis, so the result will guide the remaining 6 runs. Those runs can then vary the RNA encoder (scGPT or PCA) with the better fusion method. Expected cost is similar to config_029, about 4.5–5.5 GPU hours. Weighted fusion should add little overhead over concat.

1) Evidence: the transformer aggregator clearly beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). ImageNet ViT-L clearly beats ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion is marginally ahead of concat (0.725 vs 0.721, F1 0.685 vs 0.681), which is too small a gap to read much into. The RNA encoder is the main design choice still untested: every run so far used scvi_n200. 2) This run keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) and swaps scvi_n200 for scGPT. That isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model RNA embedding beats the scVI latent. 3) Best use of the budget: the RNA encoder is now the largest source of uncertainty with clear upside, and the change is applied on top of the strongest known configuration. If it wins, the remaining runs can refine around it. If it loses, we can try pca_n2000 (config_012) or return to scvi variants. Expected cost: roughly similar to or slightly above config_050's 3.6 GPU hours, about 4–5 GPU hours, since scGPT embeddings are larger than scVI's 200 dimensions.

1) Evidence: transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points with ResNet50. ImageNet ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3.3 points. Weighted fusion is slightly ahead of concat (0.725 vs 0.721, consistent in F1), so config_050 (scVI, ViT-L, transformer, weighted) is the current best at 0.725. Swapping scVI for scGPT in that setup dropped accuracy to 0.520, so the RNA encoder matters a lot. The third encoder, pca_n2000, is still untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best image encoder, aggregation and fusion fixed and swaps only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. It answers whether PCA features can match or beat scVI. 3) The RNA encoder is the remaining design choice with large measured impact and unknown value, so this has high upside while staying close to the proven setup. The architecture matches the recent multiprofile ViT-L transformer runs (2.9–4.7 GPU hours). The wider 2000-dimensional PCA input may add a little cost, so I expect roughly 3.5–5 GPU hours, a moderate cost similar to config_050.

1) Evidence: Every run so far is multiprofile. Within that space the RNA encoder matters a lot: scVI (0.725) beat PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520) with the ViT-L image encoder. ViT-L beat ResNet50 (0.721 vs 0.688), transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632), and weighted fusion is slightly ahead of concat (0.725 vs 0.721, F1 0.685 vs 0.681). The best known recipe is scVI + ViT-L + weighted fusion (config_050). The profile setting is the one major design axis not yet tested. 2) Test: config_028 keeps the best scVI + ViT-L + weighted recipe but uses singleprofile input. This shows how much multiprofile aggregation actually contributes, and whether a simpler, less noisy single-profile model can match or beat it. 3) Rationale: with 3 runs left, resolving an untested core axis on the strongest backbone is more informative than small variants that are likely to underperform, such as ResNet50 or avgpool versions. Expected cost is low, likely about 2–3 GPU hours, below the multiprofile runs, because it skips profile aggregation.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 at 0.725 accuracy (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, multiprofile). The history points the same way on several choices. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool, ViT-L beats ResNet50, and multiprofile beats single-profile. Weighted and concat fusion are about equal. The RNA encoder is the most sensitive choice: scVI gave 0.72, PCA 0.59 and scGPT 0.52, so a poor RNA branch can badly hurt the fused model. The open question is whether even scVI adds signal beyond the ViT-L image branch, or whether images carry most of the information. 2) Test: config_045 is image-only ViT-L with transformer aggregation over multiple profiles. It isolates the image branch's contribution. If it comes close to or beats 0.725, the last experiment should focus on image-centric variants. If it falls clearly short, the multimodal scVI + ViT-L design is confirmed and the final run can refine around config_050. 3) Why this one: the remaining single-step changes to config_050 look likely to score lower. ResNet50 (config_008) and avgpool (config_015) have each underperformed their alternatives before. This modality ablation is the most informative unexplored question that still has a plausible chance of matching the best. Expected cost: below the 3.6–4.7 GPU hours of the ViT-L multimodal runs, since there is no RNA encoder or fusion, though multiprofile transformer aggregation keeps it above the single-profile runs.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 (scVI RNA, ViT-L images, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Each component has been checked one at a time. scVI clearly beats scGPT and PCA. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). ViT-L beats ResNet50. Weighted fusion is slightly better than concat. Multiprofile beats singleprofile. Every untested multimodal neighbour swaps in a component that has already lost, so none is likely to beat 0.725. Example: config_008 swaps ViT-L back to ResNet50 and probably lands near 0.69. The main untested question is how much each modality contributes. Image-only scored just 0.26, so most of the signal seems to come from RNA, but we have never measured RNA alone. 2) Test: config_014 is the RNA-only version of the best setup (scVI, multiprofile, transformer). If it matches or beats 0.725, the image branch is adding noise and RNA-focused variants are the better final bet. If it scores well below, the fusion gain is real and config_050 is near the best for this space. 3) Why this experiment: it is the only remaining option with a real, if modest, chance of beating the incumbent, and it still informs the last experiment. Expected cost is low, roughly 1 to 2 GPU hours, since there is no image encoder. That is well below the 3.6 to 5 GPU hours of the multimodal runs.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_050 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Among the design choices, scVI clearly beats PCA and scGPT, and transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 0.033 under concat fusion. Weighted fusion gave a small gain over concat with ViT-L. 2) Test: config_008 keeps every winning choice (scVI, transformer, multiprofile, weighted fusion) and only swaps the image encoder to ResNet50. This checks whether weighted fusion closes the image-encoder gap. ResNet50 is the one strong-component alternative not yet paired with weighted fusion. 3) Why this is the best final use: every other untested option includes a choice already shown to be clearly inferior (avgpool, PCA, scGPT, singleprofile or unimodal). This makes config_008 the remaining configuration with the best realistic chance of matching or beating 0.725. Expected cost is moderate, about 4-5 GPU hours, similar to the other multiprofile transformer runs (3.6-5.2 GPU hours).

1) No experiments have been completed, so there is no evidence on modality, profile setting, encoders, aggregation or fusion. Priors suggest that multimodal inputs, multiprofile context and learned (transformer) aggregation are the most likely high-accuracy structure. Encoder choice is the most uncertain factor. 2) Config_003 tests that likely-strong structure (multimodal, multiprofile, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) using the compact scVI-200 RNA embedding and ResNet50 images. It gives a strong anchor to compare against later. Next steps can include single-modality or singleprofile ablations, avgpool vs transformer, and upgrades to scGPT or ViT-L. 3) It probes the most promising region without paying for the largest encoders up front. Expected cost is moderate: multiprofile aggregation plus multimodal processing, but with smaller representations. It should be noticeably cheaper than ViT-L or scGPT variants such as config_015.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. config_003 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200 + resnet50, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.713 accuracy and 0.695 F1 for 6.22 GPU hours. A single point says nothing yet about which components drive performance. 2) This experiment keeps everything fixed except the image encoder, swapping resnet50 for imagenet_vit_l. It cleanly tests whether a larger pretrained image representation improves accuracy. The image encoder is likely one of the most influential design choices, and the answer will guide the image-side choice for the remaining multimodal and image-only configurations. 3) It changes one factor around the current best, so it both explores and exploits, and it has a good chance of producing a new best. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_003, roughly 1.3-1.6x or about 8-10 GPU hours, because ViT-L is larger. That cost is justified because this encoder is plausibly part of the top-performing configuration.

1. Evidence: Only two experiments are done, and both used scVI RNA, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L raised validation accuracy from 0.713 to 0.725 and cut cost from 6.22 to 3.60 GPU hours. F1 was slightly lower (0.685 vs 0.695), so the image-encoder advantage is real but modest. The largest open uncertainty is the RNA encoder, since only scVI has been tried. 2. Test: Keep the current best setup (ViT-L, multiprofile, transformer, weighted fusion) and swap scVI for scGPT. This isolates whether a foundation-model RNA encoder improves the RNA side of the fusion. 3. Why now: A one-factor change on the leading configuration both exploits the best result and resolves a major untested design axis. If scGPT helps, later runs can tune aggregation and fusion around it. If not, pca_n2000 or the scVI fusion and aggregation variants are next. Expected cost is moderate: similar to or somewhat above config_018's 3.6 GPU hours, because scGPT embeddings are larger, but likely below config_003's 6.2.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the factor with the largest observed effect so far. With the same vit_l, transformer and weighted backbone, scvi_n200 reached 0.725 accuracy while scgpt reached only 0.520. The image encoder mattered much less: vit_l was slightly better than resnet50 on accuracy (0.725 vs 0.713) and was cheaper (3.6 vs 6.2 GPU h). pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. 2) Test: config_002 keeps the best configuration (config_018) fixed and swaps scvi_n200 for pca_n2000. This shows whether a simpler PCA representation matches or beats scVI. 3) Why now: settling the most influential design choice early decides which RNA encoder anchors the later aggregation and fusion tests (avgpool vs transformer, concat vs weighted). It also has a real chance of producing a new best. Expected cost is moderate, about 3-4.5 GPU hours, similar to config_018 and well below the resnet50 run. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add a little cost.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder so far (0.713–0.725 accuracy, versus 0.586 for pca_n2000 and 0.520 for scgpt). The two image encoders are close: imagenet_vit_l has slightly higher accuracy (0.725) and resnet50 slightly higher F1. Vit_l was also cheaper here (3.60 vs 6.22 GPU hours). All four runs used transformer aggregation with weighted fusion, so aggregation and fusion are completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup so far (scvi_n200, vit_l, weighted fusion) and changes only aggregation from transformer to avgpool. That isolates whether the transformer aggregator is actually needed. 3) Aggregation is a major untested design choice, and a clean single-variable comparison against the current best will guide the remaining 5 experiments. Fusion can be tested next with config_042 or a concat counterpart. Expected cost is low: avgpool should be cheaper than transformer aggregation, so likely under the 3.6 GPU hours of config_018.

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, at 0.713–0.725 versus 0.586 for PCA and 0.520 for scGPT. The best result so far is config_018 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool with this setup (0.725 vs 0.706), and its F1 was also higher. ViT-L and ResNet50 were close (0.725 vs 0.713), and ViT-L was cheaper. The fusion method is the one major design choice never tested: every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) This experiment: config_042 keeps the best setup and changes only fusion to concat. It isolates whether concat fusion can beat weighted fusion. 3) Why now: it directly exploits the leading configuration while closing the largest remaining uncertainty, so the result is easy to interpret. It also tells the remaining 3 experiments whether to keep weighted fusion. Expected cost is moderate, similar to config_018 at about 3.5–5 GPU hours, since concat fusion adds little overhead compared with weighted fusion.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the best RNA encoder (0.71-0.725 vs 0.52 for scgpt and 0.59 for pca). Within the scvi multiprofile family, the best result is 0.725 for config_018 (ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion). Swapping in concat (0.721), ResNet50 (0.713) or avgpool (0.706) gave only small drops, so local tuning around config_018 is close to exhausted. The main untested choice is modality: all six runs were multimodal, so we do not know how much the image branch actually adds. 2) This test: an RNA-only model with scvi_n200 and transformer aggregation over multiple profiles. It shows whether the RNA signal alone matches or beats the multimodal best (the image features may add noise) or falls clearly short (the image branch is necessary). That decides how to spend the last two runs: on image and fusion variants, or on RNA-only and profile-setting variants. 3) Why now: it addresses the largest remaining uncertainty and has a realistic chance of reaching about 0.72 or more, since scvi drives performance. With no image encoder it should be cheaper than the multimodal runs, roughly 2-3 GPU hours versus 3.6-6.2.

1) Evidence: The best result so far is config_018 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy, 3.6 GPU h). Swapping single components around it changes accuracy only slightly: concat fusion gave 0.721, ResNet50 gave 0.713 and avgpool gave 0.706. scGPT and PCA RNA encoders were clearly worse. The profile setting has never been tested; every multimodal run so far used multiprofile. 2) Test: config_037 keeps the best encoders and fusion but uses single-profile input with no aggregation. This isolates whether multiprofile aggregation is really needed. It is the main remaining unexplored design axis, and the single-profile model could match or beat the current best. 3) Value: The other close neighbours (ResNet50 + concat, avgpool + concat) recombine choices already shown to be slightly inferior, so they are unlikely to set a new best. This run should be cheaper than the multiprofile runs, roughly 1.5–3 GPU h, because there is no aggregation over profiles. Its result will also guide the last two experiments: refine around single-profile if it is competitive, otherwise around the multiprofile config_018.

1. Evidence: The strongest region is clear. scVI beats pca_n2000 by about 0.14 and scGPT by about 0.20. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool by about 0.019. Multiprofile beats singleprofile by about 0.19, and multimodal beats RNA-only by about 0.07. Within this region, the best result is config_018 (ViT-L, weighted, 0.725). The neighbouring configs config_042 (ViT-L, concat, 0.721) and config_003 (ResNet50, weighted, 0.713) score within about 0.012 of it. Those gaps are small enough to fall within run-to-run noise. 2. What it tests: config_033 (scVI + ResNet50 + transformer + concat) is the only untested scVI/transformer/multiprofile multimodal combination. It completes the image-encoder by fusion comparison, showing whether ResNet50 pairs better with concat fusion than with weighted fusion. 3. Why it is the best use of the slot: every other remaining option drops at least one component that clearly helped. Those are either scGPT or PCA instead of scVI, avgpool instead of transformer, singleprofile, or a single modality, so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This makes config_033 the highest-probability, if modest, chance of a new best. Expected cost is relatively high, around 5-6 GPU hours, similar to config_003 (6.22 h). That is justified because it is the remaining candidate most likely to compete for the top spot.

1) Evidence: the strongest region is clear. It is multimodal, multiprofile, with an scVI-n200 RNA encoder and an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder. The best run is config_018 (transformer, weighted) at 0.725, followed by config_042 (concat) at 0.721 and config_016 (avgpool) at 0.706. Swapping in scGPT or PCA for RNA dropped accuracy sharply (0.52–0.59). Single-profile and RNA-only runs were also clearly worse, and ResNet50 is slightly behind ViT-L. 2) This experiment: config_007 is the only untested scVI + ViT-L multiprofile combination left. It tests avgpool aggregation together with concat fusion. That combination has not been run, and fusion choice could interact with how profiles are pooled. 3) Why it is the best final use: it stays in the proven high-accuracy region, so it is the most plausible way to match or slightly beat 0.725. The alternatives look weaker. Image-only or other-encoder options have weak or negative evidence, and the remaining scVI + ResNet50 avgpool variants pair the weaker image encoder with the weaker aggregation. Expected cost is moderate, around 4.5–5 GPU hours, similar to config_016 and config_042.

1. Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been run, so every design choice is uncertain. These choices are modality, single vs. multiple profiles, RNA and image encoder, aggregation and fusion. Prior expectation is that combining both modalities and aggregating multiple profiles should give the strongest signal, but this is unconfirmed here. 2. What it tests: config_001 is a multimodal, multiprofile setup built from the cheaper components: scVI-200 RNA embeddings, a ResNet50 image encoder, avgpool aggregation and simple concat fusion. Its accuracy will show whether the multimodal + multiprofile direction is promising before paying for more expensive parts. 3. Why now: It is a mid-cost anchor that later experiments can compare against by changing one factor at a time. Candidate swaps include ViT-L for ResNet50, transformer for avgpool, weighted for concat, scGPT or PCA for scVI, and single-modality ablations. This leaves 9 experiments to exploit what it reveals. Expected relative cost: moderate. It costs more than single-profile or unimodal runs because of multiprofile and multimodal processing, but clearly less than ViT-L or transformer-aggregation variants.

1) Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile config_001 (scVI-200 RNA, ResNet50 images, avgpool aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.632 accuracy and 0.607 F1 at 7.27 GPU hours. That gives a reasonable baseline in what is probably the strongest region of the space, but every design axis is still untested. 2) Test: config_049 changes exactly one factor, swapping avgpool for transformer aggregation. Any difference can therefore be attributed to how the multiple profiles are combined. A learned, attention-based aggregator could plausibly beat mean pooling, while the RNA encoder, image encoder and fusion choices stay fixed. 3) Why now: aggregation is likely a high-impact choice that affects many of the remaining multiprofile configurations, so settling it early guides much of the remaining 8-experiment budget. Swapping in the ViT-L image encoder instead would likely cost more. Expected cost: moderately higher than config_001 because of the transformer aggregator, roughly 8-10 GPU hours, which is less than the larger-encoder alternatives.

Evidence: with everything else held fixed (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat), transformer aggregation clearly beat avgpool on both accuracy (0.688 vs 0.632) and F1 (0.659 vs 0.607). It was also cheaper (5.16 vs 7.27 GPU h), so transformer aggregation is the current anchor. The image encoder is still untested and is a high-impact choice, since ViT-L representations are much richer than ResNet50. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_049) and changes only the image encoder to imagenet_vit_l. That cleanly measures the encoder's effect and exploits the strongest known direction. It is the best use of a limited budget because the encoder choice likely moves accuracy more than fusion type, and the answer shapes most of the remaining search. Expected cost is moderately higher than config_049, roughly 1.3-1.8x, because ViT-L features are larger, though transformer aggregation should keep it under about 8 GPU h. If the gain is small, later experiments can return to cheaper ResNet50 variants such as weighted fusion or scGPT.

1) Evidence: with the scVI RNA encoder and concat fusion fixed, transformer aggregation beat avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with ResNet50). Swapping ResNet50 for ImageNet ViT-L under transformer aggregation raised accuracy to 0.721 (F1 0.681), the current best (config_018). Fusion has never been varied: every run used concat. The RNA encoder alternatives (PCA, scGPT) are also untested. 2) Test: config_007 matches the best configuration except for weighted fusion instead of concat. This one-factor change isolates the effect of fusion on top of the strongest setup, and F1 can confirm whether any gain is real. 3) Why now: it directly exploits the best configuration found so far while resolving an unexplored design choice that affects every future multimodal candidate. Weighted fusion only adds learned modality weights to the same encoders, so I expect it to cost about the same as config_018 (roughly 4.5-5.5 GPU hours). That is cheaper than the avgpool baseline run and no more expensive than switching to a heavier encoder such as scGPT, which can be tested next on whichever fusion wins.

1. Evidence: Every run so far uses the scvi_n200 RNA encoder. Three image/aggregation/fusion choices have clear evidence. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 5.6 points (0.688 vs 0.632). ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 3.3 points (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion edged out concat (0.725 vs 0.721, with F1 also slightly higher), though that gap is small. The biggest untested axis is the RNA encoder. 2. Test: config_024 keeps the best-known setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, weighted fusion) and swaps in scGPT. Changing only one factor isolates whether a pretrained single-cell foundation model improves the RNA representation over scvi_n200. 3. Why now: this extends the strongest direction while reducing uncertainty on the main open design choice. If scGPT helps, the remaining budget can refine around it. If it does not, pca_n2000 (config_005) is the natural next comparison. Expected cost: similar to or somewhat above config_007 (3.6 GPU hours), roughly 4-6 GPU hours, because scGPT embeddings may be larger. That still stays within the range of earlier runs.

1) Evidence: transformer aggregation clearly beats avgpool (0.688 vs 0.632 with resnet50). imagenet_vit_l beats resnet50 (0.721 vs 0.688). Weighted fusion is slightly ahead of concat (0.725 vs 0.721), a small difference. Swapping the RNA encoder to scgpt in the best setup collapsed accuracy to 0.520, so the RNA encoder is a high-impact choice. pca_n2000 is the only RNA encoder not yet tested. 2) config_005 keeps the best setup (multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted) and changes only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000. This shows whether scvi_n200 is truly the best RNA representation or whether a higher-dimensional PCA input does better. 3) It is the factor with the largest remaining uncertainty and a plausible chance of a new best result, while staying in the strongest region of the search space. Expected cost is moderate, roughly 3.5-5 GPU hours, similar to config_007. The 2000-dimensional PCA input may add a little cost over the 200-dimensional scVI input, but no image-side cost is added.

1) Evidence: every run so far has used multiprofile. The best result is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, acc 0.725, F1 0.685). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.06, ViT-L beat ResNet50, and weighted fusion was slightly ahead of concat. scVI is clearly the best RNA encoder, well ahead of PCA (0.586) and scGPT (0.520). 2) Untested choice: whether to aggregate across multiple profiles at all. This run keeps the strongest components (scVI, ViT-L, weighted fusion) and switches to singleprofile, which directly tests that axis. avgpool variants such as config_012 are unlikely to win given the earlier aggregation gap. 3) Why now: single-profile models skip the costly aggregation step, so this should be the cheapest multimodal run yet, likely below the roughly 3.6 to 4.7 GPU hours of earlier ViT-L runs. If it matches or beats config_007, the last runs can focus on cheaper single-profile variants. If it falls short, it confirms multiprofile with transformer as the backbone, and I would use the final runs to test image-only and RNA-only references (configs 029 and 040).

Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Within this neighbourhood, scVI clearly beats scGPT and PCA, ViT-L beats ResNet50, and weighted fusion edges concat by a small margin. The weakest-tested choice in the top region is aggregation. Transformer beat avgpool only once, with ResNet50 and concat fusion (0.688 vs 0.632), and avgpool was never tried with ViT-L features. This experiment keeps the best configuration and swaps transformer for avgpool. It checks whether that earlier gap holds with the stronger image encoder, since richer ViT-L embeddings could make simple pooling competitive or better. It is the most direct exploit-plus-uncertainty test left, and the other neighbours (ResNet50, PCA, scGPT, single-profile) already have strong negative evidence. Expected cost is moderate to high, roughly 4–7 GPU hours. That is similar to the earlier multiprofile runs, and the one avgpool run (config_001) cost more than the transformer runs. The cost is acceptable because this is one of the few remaining candidates with a real chance of beating 0.725.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725 acc / 0.685 F1). Its close neighbours scored slightly lower: concat fusion gave 0.721 and avgpool aggregation gave 0.706. Switching to ResNet50 cost about 0.03 and multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. So the remaining multimodal variants (config_044, config_026) are likely to land around 0.69 to 0.71 and unlikely to beat the best. The main untested question is how much each modality contributes. Swapping scVI for scGPT or PCA cut accuracy sharply (0.52 and 0.59), and weighted fusion did not protect against this. That shows the RNA branch strongly shapes results, but we still do not know whether a ViT-L image-only model is competitive. 2) This experiment tests image-only ViT-L with multiprofile transformer aggregation, the strongest image-side setup. It shows whether RNA adds signal on top of the images or only adds noise. 3) It is the only remaining option with a plausible chance of exceeding 0.725, and it informs how to use the final experiment. Expected cost is low to moderate (about 2 to 3.5 GPU hours), below the full multimodal runs, because no RNA branch or fusion is trained.

1) Evidence: the best result is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Each design choice is fairly well supported. scVI beats PCA and scGPT, ViT-L beats ResNet50, transformer beats avgpool, and multiprofile beats singleprofile. That isolates the effect of fusion directly. 3) It is the best next use of budget because it closes the largest untested gap among the design axes (fusion) with a clean one-variable comparison. It is also a plausible improvement on the top configuration. Testing scGPT can follow once the fusion choice is settled.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is config_007 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) at 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. Three changes have shown consistent gains. Multiprofile beat singleprofile, transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 0.056, and ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 0.033. Weighted versus concat fusion differed by only about 0.004, so fusion looks like a minor factor. The main gap is the RNA encoder. scGPT has never been tested, although RNA is clearly the stronger modality (image-only scored 0.33, RNA-only 0.59). 2. This run swaps the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT and keeps everything else the same as the current best. Any change in accuracy or F1 can therefore be attributed to the RNA representation. 3. Under a limited budget, this is the best next step for two reasons. It probes the largest unexplored design choice, in the modality that matters most. It also tests that choice in the strongest known setting, so it could directly produce a new best configuration. Smaller questions, such as fusion type or another aggregation comparison, are less likely to shift performance meaningfully.

1) Evidence: the best result so far is multimodal scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion (0.725 acc, 0.685 F1). Moving from avgpool to transformer aggregation gave a clear gain of about 0.056, and ViT-L beat ResNet50 by about 0.03. But the only image-only run (ResNet50, avgpool) was weak at 0.33, and no RNA-only model has used transformer aggregation or scVI. So it is unclear how much of the top score comes from the image modality versus RNA with transformer aggregation. 2) This experiment is an RNA-only ablation of the best pipeline: scVI, multiprofile, transformer, with the image branch removed. If it scores near 0.72, fusion adds little. If it scores much lower, the image branch genuinely contributes. It also shows whether the transformer gain holds without images. 3) Small fusion tweaks (concat vs weighted differed by about 0.004) or exploitative variants carry little information. This single-factor ablation resolves a central design question, whether multimodality is necessary, before more budget is spent refining fusion or image encoders.

1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about any design choice: modality, RNA or image encoder, profile setting, aggregation or fusion. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA with 2000 components, no aggregation or fusion) is the simplest, lowest-variance baseline in the space. It gives a reference point for the RNA modality. Later experiments can each change one factor against it: the encoder (scVI or scGPT, config_004 and config_007), the profile setting and aggregation (config_002 and config_003), or adding images (config_016). 3) With a limited budget and no prior information, a cheap and interpretable anchor gets the most out of every later comparison. Starting with a complex multimodal or multiprofile model would mix several factors together and make the gains hard to attribute.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest configuration in the search space as a reference point: RNA-only, single-profile, with a PCA RNA encoder (2000 components) and no image encoder, aggregation or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.485, with a validation F1 of 0.464 as supporting evidence. Because no other experiments have been run, this is only an initial baseline and cannot show whether the encoder, modality or profile setting helps or hurts performance. It is still unknown whether other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), multiprofile settings with aggregation, or adding image features would improve on it. Its single-run variance is also unknown, so later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons against it should treat small differences cautiously.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: the only result so far is the RNA-only, single-profile PCA baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). We know nothing yet about how much signal the image modality carries, and image-based configurations make up most of the remaining search space (image-only and all multimodal options). 2. Test: config_010 keeps everything else at its simplest (single-profile, no aggregation, no fusion) and swaps RNA for images with a ResNet50 encoder. This gives a clean single-profile image baseline to compare directly with config_001 for the modality question. 3. Why now: establishing whether images are weaker, comparable or stronger than RNA is the highest-leverage uncertainty. It tells us whether to spend later budget on multimodal fusion and image-encoder comparisons (for example ResNet50 vs ViT-L), or to focus on RNA encoders and multiprofile aggregation. Tuning RNA encoders or aggregation first would leave this larger structural question open.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 tested an image-only, single-profile configuration with a ResNet50 image encoder and no RNA encoder, aggregation or fusion, as a first image baseline to compare against the RNA-only PCA baseline (llm_summary_001). It reached a validation accuracy of 0.208 (F1 0.172), well below the RNA-only baseline (accuracy 0.485, F1 0.464). This suggests that this particular image setup carries less class-relevant signal than PCA-encoded RNA. However, the two runs differ in both modality and encoder, so the gap cannot be attributed to the image modality alone rather than to ResNet50 features specifically. It also remains unknown whether other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L), multiprofile aggregation, or fusion with RNA would make image features useful (the latter as complementary rather than redundant information), and single-run variance has not been measured.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: Only two single-profile baselines exist. RNA-only PCA reached 0.485 accuracy (F1 0.464), and image-only ResNet50 reached 0.208 (F1 0.172). So RNA is currently the stronger modality. Whether multiprofile input with aggregation helps is completely untested, even though that choice applies to most remaining configurations, across both modalities and fusion. 2. Test: This keeps the strongest baseline fixed (RNA-only, PCA encoder) and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multiprofile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). That isolates whether combining multiple profiles adds class-relevant signal. 3. Why now: It is a clean one-factor comparison against the best result so far. A gain would point to a broadly applicable direction and justify trying transformer aggregation next. No gain would let us deprioritize many multiprofile configurations. Either outcome cuts uncertainty about a high-impact design choice before we spend budget on encoder or fusion variants.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 was a one-factor comparison against the RNA-only PCA (2000-component) baseline (llm_summary_001), changing only the profile setting from single-profile to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.485 to 0.591, and F1 rose from 0.464 to 0.573, making this the best result so far and suggesting that pooling multiple profiles adds class-relevant signal for PCA-encoded RNA. Because multiprofile input and avgpool aggregation were introduced together, the gain cannot yet be split between them, and run-to-run variance is unmeasured, though a gain of about 0.1 is unlikely to be noise alone. Several questions remain untested: whether the benefit carries over to image-only or fusion settings and to other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), and whether richer aggregation (e.g., transformer) improves on avgpool.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the RNA-only PCA multiprofile run with avgpool (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1) clearly beat its single-profile counterpart (0.485 acc). That makes multiprofile input the strongest direction so far. Because multiprofile input and avgpool were introduced together, it is still unknown how much the aggregation method matters. Image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.208), so adding fusion now is lower priority. 2) Test: config_003 keeps everything from the current best run fixed (RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile) and changes only avgpool to transformer aggregation. This isolates whether a learned set aggregator extracts more signal from multiple profiles than simple averaging. 3) Value: aggregation is a choice shared by every remaining multiprofile configuration, across RNA-only, image-only and multimodal settings. Resolving it now builds on the strongest evidence and prunes a large part of the search space. Comparing encoders (scVI, scGPT) or adding fusion can then use the better aggregator. Any small difference should be read alongside F1, given unmeasured run-to-run variance.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 was a one-factor comparison against the best run so far (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, PCA-2000, multiprofile). It changed only the aggregation, from avgpool to a transformer set aggregator. Validation accuracy fell from 0.591 to 0.519 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.480, which suggests that, in this setting and with this configuration, transformer aggregation underperforms simple averaging; it still stays slightly above the single-profile baseline (0.485 accuracy, 0.464 F1), weakly hinting that multiprofile input helps somewhat even without avgpool. The result comes from a single run with unmeasured variance, and it is unknown whether the transformer was limited by training budget, hyperparameters or data size, or whether the ranking holds for other RNA encoders (scVI, scGPT), image-only or fusion settings, so avgpool is the provisionally preferred aggregator rather than a confirmed one.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only PCA-2000 with multiprofile avgpool (0.591 acc, 0.573 F1). Multiprofile avgpool clearly beat single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). The ResNet50 image-only baseline was weak (0.208), so adding images is not an obvious win. The RNA encoder choice is still completely untested, and all RNA results so far use PCA. 2) This experiment keeps the best setting (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and changes only the encoder, from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. It tests whether a learned, lower-dimensional representation improves on PCA. 3) The encoder choice affects every RNA-only and multimodal configuration, so this answer narrows a large part of the remaining search space. The comparison is a clean one-factor test against the current best. It is also a plausible candidate to set a new best, which balances exploration and exploitation better than testing fusion with weak image features.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 was a one-factor comparison against the previous best (llm_summary_003: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, PCA-2000), changing only the RNA encoder from PCA-2000 to scVI-200. Validation accuracy rose from 0.591 to 0.650 and F1 from 0.573 to 0.628, making this the new best configuration. Because only the encoder changed, this suggests that the scVI-200 representation is more useful than PCA-2000 in this setting. However, scVI differs from PCA in both being learned and being lower-dimensional, so the gain cannot be attributed to either property alone. Several points remain uncertain: the result comes from a single run with unmeasured variance (though a gain of about 0.06 is moderately large); it is untested whether the encoder advantage holds for single-profile, transformer aggregation or fusion settings, or how scVI compares with scGPT; and whether adding image features to this stronger RNA representation would help is still unknown, given the weak ResNet50 image-only baseline.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: In the RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setting, the RNA encoder has had a large effect. Switching from PCA-2000 to scVI-200 raised accuracy from 0.591 to 0.650 (F1 0.573 to 0.628), the best result so far. Avgpool has been provisionally preferred over the transformer aggregator. The third RNA encoder, scGPT, has never been tested, so the encoder ranking is still incomplete. 2. What this tests: config_008 changes only the encoder from scVI-200 to scGPT, keeping RNA-only, multiprofile and avgpool fixed. This isolates whether a pretrained foundation-model representation beats or trails scVI. It finishes the encoder comparison in the strongest known setting, and it may also produce a new best configuration. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: Every multimodal configuration depends on choosing an RNA backbone. Image signal has so far been weak (0.208 accuracy with ResNet50). Settling the RNA encoder first means later fusion experiments can be anchored on the strongest RNA representation, which avoids spending budget on multimodal runs built on a suboptimal encoder. It is a clean one-factor test that mixes exploitation and exploration.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 changed only the RNA encoder relative to the best run (llm_summary_005: RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool, scVI-200), switching from scVI-200 to scGPT, which completes the RNA encoder comparison in this setting. Validation accuracy fell to 0.530 (F1 0.515), below both scVI-200 (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1) and PCA-2000 (llm_summary_003: 0.591 accuracy, 0.573 F1) under the same settings, though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.485). This gives a provisional encoder ranking for this setting of scVI-200 > PCA-2000 > scGPT, which supports anchoring later fusion experiments on scVI-200. It remains uncertain why scGPT underperformed (e.g., how its embeddings were extracted or adapted, dimensionality, or training budget), whether the ranking holds for single-profile, transformer-aggregation or fusion settings, and how large single-run variance is, so the ranking should be treated as preliminary rather than confirmed.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: all RNA-only runs are informative but not settled. Multiprofile avgpool beat single-profile (0.591 vs 0.485). Avgpool beat transformer aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519). scVI-200 is the best RNA encoder so far (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1, ahead of PCA and scGPT). The main untested question is whether adding image features helps at all. The only image evidence is a weak single-profile ResNet50 image-only run (0.208), which cannot show whether image features add complementary signal when fused with RNA. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup fixed (scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool) and adds only one thing: ResNet50 image features through simple concat fusion. The comparison with config_005 therefore isolates the effect of adding the image modality. ResNet50 is used rather than ViT-L so that the image encoder is the one we already have a baseline for, and concat is the simplest fusion reference. 3) This is the best use of the next experiment because it exploits the strongest configuration while testing the central design choice in the study, multimodal versus unimodal. Either outcome guides the remaining budget. A gain would justify exploring image encoders and fusion types. No gain or a drop would suggest putting effort into RNA-side refinements or testing ViT-L features first.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 was a one-factor comparison against the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_005: multiprofile, avgpool, scVI-200). The only change was adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion, which tests whether the image modality adds complementary signal. Validation accuracy fell slightly from 0.650 to 0.632 and F1 from 0.628 to 0.607, so in this setup adding ResNet50 features via concat gave no benefit and may have slightly hurt. Both values still exceed every other run, including PCA-2000 multiprofile (0.591). The drop of about 0.02 is small and comes from single runs with unmeasured variance, so it may be noise rather than a real degradation. It is also unknown whether the null result reflects the image modality itself, the weak ResNet50 features (image-only reached only 0.208), the simple concat fusion, or untuned training. Other image encoders (e.g., ViT-L) and other fusion methods therefore remain untested before multimodal fusion can be judged unhelpful.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: scVI-200 with multiprofile avgpool is the best run so far (0.650 accuracy). Adding ResNet50 image features through concat fusion (config_030) slightly lowered accuracy to 0.632. That null result is ambiguous. ResNet50 features look weak (image-only accuracy was 0.208), so we cannot tell whether the image modality adds nothing or whether this particular encoder is the problem. 2. What this tests: config_036 changes only the image encoder relative to config_030, from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Everything else stays the same: scVI-200, multiprofile, avgpool and concat. This isolates whether a stronger image representation can add signal that complements the strong RNA setup. 3. Why it is the best next experiment: the image encoder is the largest untested factor and the most likely cause of the failed fusion. Testing fusion method first (weighted, config_031) with the same weak ResNet50 features would be less decisive. This run either uncovers a multimodal gain above 0.650 or makes it more credible that the image modality adds little, which would guide how much of the remaining budget to spend on multimodal configurations.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_008 was a one-factor comparison against llm_summary_007 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, avgpool, concat fusion), changing only the image encoder from ResNet50 to ImageNet ViT-L. Validation accuracy rose from 0.632 to 0.715 and F1 from 0.607 to 0.687, making this the new best configuration and the first multimodal run to exceed the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_005: 0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). This suggests that, in this setting, the ViT-L image representation adds signal that complements scVI-200 RNA features, and that the earlier null fusion result was more likely tied to the ResNet50 features than to the image modality itself. It remains uncertain how much of the gain comes from ViT-L features alone versus their complementarity with RNA, because no ViT-L image-only baseline exists; whether other fusion methods (e.g., weighted) or aggregators would add further gains; and how large single-run variance is, though a gain of about 0.06–0.08 is moderately large.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best run so far is config_036 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat), at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Earlier single-factor comparisons favoured multiprofile over single-profile, avgpool over transformer, scVI-200 over PCA and scGPT, and ViT-L over ResNet50. Fusion is the only design axis never tested: every multimodal run used concat, so we don't know whether concat is limiting the gain from adding images. 2) This run changes only the fusion method, from concat to weighted, keeping everything else as in config_036. It shows whether a learned weighting of the two modalities adds to the RNA–image complementarity seen with ViT-L. The result is useful either way: a gain extends the best setup, and a drop or tie supports concat as the default. 3) It explores an untested factor while building on the strongest configuration, so it has a good chance of an immediate improvement. A ViT-L image-only baseline (config_014) would help explain where the multimodal gain comes from, but it is unlikely to beat the current best. Settling the fusion choice first is the better use of limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_009 was a one-factor comparison against the current best run (llm_summary_008: multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200, ViT-L, avgpool, concat), changing only the fusion method from concat to weighted. It was the first test of the fusion axis, since all earlier multimodal runs used concat. Validation accuracy was 0.706 versus 0.715, and F1 was 0.667 versus 0.687, so weighted fusion did not improve on concat and was slightly worse, especially on F1. It still exceeded the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_005: 0.650 accuracy). This makes concat the provisional default fusion choice, but the gap (about 0.009 accuracy and 0.02 F1) is small and comes from single runs with unmeasured variance, so it may be a tie rather than a real disadvantage. It also remains unknown whether weighted fusion was limited by tuning or training budget, whether the fusion ranking holds with other encoders or aggregators, and how much of the multimodal gain comes from ViT-L features alone, since no ViT-L image-only baseline has been run.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: The best run is config_036 (scVI-200 + ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat) at 0.715 accuracy and 0.687 F1. Weighted fusion (config_037) roughly tied it. Swapping ResNet50 for ViT-L raised multimodal accuracy by about 0.08. We still cannot tell whether that gain reflects true complementarity with RNA or simply that ViT-L image features are strong on their own, because the only image-only baseline is ResNet50 single-profile (0.208). 2) What this tests: config_014 is image-only ViT-L with multiprofile and avgpool, so it differs from config_036 only by removing the RNA branch. Comparing it with config_036 (0.715) and the scVI RNA-only run config_005 (0.650) shows how much each modality contributes and whether fusion is additive or redundant. It also tests whether the multiprofile and avgpool benefit seen for RNA carries over to images. 3) Why it is the best next use of budget: This uncertainty has been flagged repeatedly and bears on how to read every multimodal result. A single clean ablation reduces it. It is more informative than exploiting nearby variants of the best configuration, such as transformer aggregation, which has already underperformed avgpool for RNA.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_010 was a modality ablation of the current best run (llm_summary_008: scVI-200 + ImageNet ViT-L, multiprofile, avgpool, concat, 0.715 accuracy). It removed only the RNA branch, giving an image-only ViT-L multiprofile avgpool model, which reached 0.332 validation accuracy (F1 0.315). That is far below both the best RNA-only run (llm_summary_005, scVI-200: 0.650) and the multimodal best (0.715), so ViT-L features alone carry only modest class signal and cannot by themselves explain the multimodal result. This is consistent with the roughly 0.065 multimodal gain over RNA-only reflecting complementary image information on top of RNA, rather than strong standalone image features. The run also improves on the only other image-only run (llm_summary_002, ResNet50 single-profile: 0.208), but that comparison changes both the encoder and the profile/aggregation setting, so it remains untested how much comes from ViT-L versus multiprofile avgpool for images. All results are single runs with unmeasured variance, which matters most for the small multimodal margins.

selection_reason: 1) No experiments have been run, so there is no evidence about which modality, encoder, profile setting, aggregation, or fusion choice matters. 2) config_001 (RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000) is the simplest, lowest-variance baseline. It gives a reference accuracy and F1 that later experiments can be compared against by changing one factor at a time: the RNA encoder (scVI, scGPT), the profile setting and aggregation (avgpool, transformer), or adding an image modality and fusion. 3) Under a limited budget, an anchor baseline makes every later result interpretable as the effect of a single design choice. Starting with a complex multimodal configuration would mix several factors together and prevent attributing gains, so the cheap, interpretable baseline is the best first experiment.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_001 tested the simplest baseline: an RNA-only, single-profile model using a PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder, with no image encoder, aggregation, or fusion. It reached a validation accuracy of 0.4849, with a supporting validation F1 of 0.4639. Because this is the first completed experiment, the result is only an initial reference point. It does not show whether other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT), multi-profile aggregation, or adding the image modality with fusion would help or hurt. Its main value is as an anchor for later one-factor-at-a-time comparisons. Its variance across seeds or splits is also unknown, so small differences in future runs should be read cautiously.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: Only one experiment is complete. The RNA-only, single-profile, PCA-2000 baseline reached 0.485 accuracy and 0.464 F1. We have no evidence yet on the main design axes: profile setting, RNA encoder, image modality, or fusion. 2. What this tests: config_002 keeps the modality and encoder fixed and changes only the profile setting, from single-profile to multi-profile with the simplest aggregation (avgpool). This isolates whether pooling multiple profiles helps. 3. Why this is the best next use of budget: Profile setting splits the search space roughly in half, since most remaining configurations are multi-profile. Its effect is likely to carry over to image-only and multimodal models. A clean one-factor comparison against config_001 will tell us whether to focus on multi-profile variants and whether to test transformer aggregation next. Encoder and modality comparisons (config_004, config_010) remain the natural follow-ups.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_002 kept the RNA-only model and PCA (n=2000) RNA encoder from llm_summary_001 fixed and changed only the profile setting, from single-profile to multi-profile with avgpool aggregation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.4849 to 0.5907 (+~0.106), and supporting validation F1 rose from 0.4639 to 0.5727 (+~0.109). Because this is a close one-factor comparison, the gain plausibly reflects moving to multi-profile input, but multi-profile and avgpool aggregation change together, so their separate contributions are unknown. Each result comes from a single run with unknown seed/split variance, and it remains untested whether the benefit holds for other aggregations (e.g., transformer), other RNA encoders, or image-only and multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence: In the RNA-only PCA setting, moving from single-profile to multi-profile with avgpool raised accuracy from 0.485 to 0.591, with a similar F1 gain. That is the strongest signal so far. However, profile setting and aggregation changed together, so we do not know whether the gain comes from multiple profiles or from avgpool specifically. 2. Test: config_003 keeps config_002 identical (RNA-only, PCA n2000, multi-profile) and swaps only avgpool for transformer aggregation. This isolates the aggregation choice. It shows whether a learned aggregator adds value or whether simple pooling is enough. 3. Why now: This builds on the most promising direction with a clean one-factor comparison. Aggregation also applies to almost every remaining multi-profile configuration, unimodal and multimodal alike, so settling it early can prune much of the search space. Encoder and modality questions can follow once the multi-profile setup is better understood.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_003 kept llm_summary_002 fixed (RNA-only, multi-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, no image encoder or fusion) and swapped only the aggregation, from avgpool to transformer, so this is a clean one-factor comparison of aggregation. Validation accuracy fell from 0.5907 to 0.5191 (about -0.072), and supporting F1 fell from 0.5727 to 0.4797 (about -0.093). This suggests that in this setting the transformer aggregator underperformed simple average pooling, though it stayed modestly above the single-profile baseline (accuracy 0.4849, F1 0.4639). That hints that part of the multi-profile benefit may hold across aggregators, but it does not separate the profile and aggregation effects. Each result comes from a single run with unknown seed and split variance, and the transformer's capacity and training settings may not have been tuned, so it remains uncertain whether learned aggregation is truly worse or just under-optimized, and whether this ranking holds for other RNA encoders, image-only models, or multimodal models.

selection_reason: 1. Evidence and uncertainty: In the clean comparisons so far, multi-profile input with avgpool aggregation is the strongest setting (acc 0.591, F1 0.573). It beat both single-profile (0.485) and transformer aggregation (0.519). The image modality is completely untested, and it is the largest open design question for a multimodal study. 2. What this tests: config_018 keeps the best RNA-only setup fixed (PCA n2000, multi-profile, avgpool) and adds a ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion. Concat is the minimal fusion choice. The result shows directly whether image features add useful signal on top of the best configuration, or whether they hurt it. 3. Why this is the best next experiment: It extends the strongest direction found so far and resolves the most consequential uncertainty in a single run. A gain would point the search toward multimodal configurations, and the image-encoder and fusion variants could then be tested one at a time. No gain would suggest focusing on RNA encoders such as scVI or scGPT. This is a one-step change from config_002, so it is easy to interpret, although results are single runs and small differences should be read cautiously.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_004 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 fixed (multi-profile, PCA n=2000 RNA encoder, avgpool aggregation) and added a ResNet50 image encoder with simple concat fusion, making the model multimodal. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6186 (about +0.028), and supporting F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6103 (about +0.038), making this the best configuration so far and an initial sign that image features may add useful signal on top of RNA. The gain is modest and comes from single runs with unknown seed and split variance, so it may fall within run-to-run noise. Adding the image encoder and the concat fusion changed together, so their separate roles are not isolated. It also remains untested how an image-only model performs, whether other image encoders or fusion methods do better, and whether the gain holds with other RNA encoders (e.g., scVI, scGPT) or aggregators.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence and uncertainty: Multi-profile input with avgpool clearly helped the RNA-only model (0.485 to 0.591). Adding ResNet50 images with concat fusion gave a further modest gain (0.619 accuracy, 0.610 F1). That gain is small, comes from single runs, and the image modality has never been tested alone, so we do not know how much signal images carry. 2) What this tests: An image-only, multi-profile ResNet50 model with avgpool matches config_018 except that RNA is removed. Together with config_002, which removes the image side, it brackets the multimodal result. If image-only is weak, images are a minor complement to RNA. If it is near or above 0.62, images drive much of the performance, and the fusion design or image encoder choice (ResNet50 vs ViT-L) deserves priority. 3) Why this is the best next experiment: It answers a basic question about how much each modality contributes, which will guide whether later budget goes to RNA encoders, image encoders or fusion methods. Testing those directly now would build on an unverified assumption about where the useful signal comes from.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_005 tested an image-only model (ResNet50, multi-profile, avgpool, no RNA or fusion), matching llm_summary_004 except that the RNA side was removed and serving as the image counterpart to the RNA-only llm_summary_002. It reached validation accuracy 0.3275 (supporting F1 0.2884), far below RNA-only multi-profile (0.5907), the multimodal model (0.6186), and even the RNA-only single-profile baseline (0.4849). This suggests that in this setup ResNet50 image features alone carry much less discriminative signal than RNA, and that RNA likely drives most of the multimodal performance, with images at most a minor complement. These are single runs with unknown seed and split variance, and the image encoder was not varied, so a weak ResNet50 representation or untuned image training cannot be ruled out (ViT-L is untested). It is also unclear whether the small multimodal gain in llm_summary_004 reflects real complementary image signal or noise.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal. RNA-only multiprofile avgpool reached 0.591 accuracy, image-only reached 0.328, and adding ResNet50 images gave only about +0.028 (0.619), which may be within noise. Multiprofile with avgpool is the best RNA setting so far, beating both single-profile and transformer aggregation. Yet every run used the PCA n2000 RNA encoder, so the RNA representation is the largest untested design choice for the dominant modality. 2) Test: config_005 swaps only the RNA encoder to scVI (n200) and keeps the best RNA-only setup fixed (multiprofile, avgpool, no image). Compared with config_002, this cleanly isolates the effect of the RNA encoder. 3) Why now: because RNA dominates, the RNA encoder choice is likely to shift performance more than image encoder or fusion tweaks. The result will guide whether later multimodal runs should use PCA or scVI, or should next test scGPT. That makes it the best use of the next experiment under a limited budget.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_006 kept the best RNA-only setup from llm_summary_002 fixed (multi-profile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion) and swapped only the RNA encoder from PCA n=2000 to scVI n=200, a clean one-factor test of the RNA representation. Validation accuracy rose from 0.5907 to 0.6501 (about +0.059), and supporting F1 rose from 0.5727 to 0.6275 (about +0.055). This RNA-only run is now the best configuration so far, above the PCA-based multimodal model llm_summary_004 (0.6186 accuracy, 0.6103 F1). This suggests the scVI representation helps in this setting and that the RNA encoder may matter more than adding ResNet50 images. Results are single runs with unknown seed and split variance, and scVI differs from PCA in both method and dimensionality (200 vs 2000), so these two factors cannot be separated. It also remains untested whether the gain carries over to multimodal fusion, other aggregators, or other encoders such as scGPT.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: RNA carries most of the signal. Image-only reached 0.328, while RNA-only multiprofile reached 0.591 with PCA. Changing the RNA encoder was one of the largest effects so far: switching PCA to scVI within the same RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool setup gave +0.059 accuracy and +0.055 F1, making config_005 the best result (0.650). Adding ResNet50 images gave only a modest, possibly noisy gain (+0.028). The third RNA encoder option, scGPT, is completely untested. 2) This experiment keeps the best known setup fixed (RNA-only, multiprofile, avgpool) and swaps only the encoder to scGPT. This is a clean one-factor comparison that completes the encoder axis (PCA vs scVI vs scGPT) under identical conditions. 3) The encoder appears to be the most important design choice, so knowing which encoder is best should come before multimodal fusion tests. Every later multimodal or fusion experiment depends on that choice. If scGPT beats scVI, the search should pivot to scGPT-based multimodal configurations. If it does not, scVI is confirmed as the base for testing whether images add value (e.g., config_030). Either outcome directly narrows the remaining search space.
experiment_summary: Experiment llm_summary_007 kept the best RNA-only setup fixed (multi-profile, avgpool, no image encoder or fusion) and swapped only the RNA encoder to scGPT, completing a one-factor comparison of the three RNA encoders. It reached validation accuracy 0.5305 (supporting F1 0.5152), well below scVI n=200 (0.6501 / 0.6275; about -0.120 accuracy) and also below PCA n=2000 (0.5907 / 0.5727; about -0.060), though still above the single-profile PCA baseline (0.4849). This suggests that in this setup scGPT embeddings are the weakest of the three RNA representations and supports scVI as the base for later multimodal and fusion tests. These are single runs with unknown seed and split variance, and scGPT likely differs from the others in embedding dimensionality, pretraining domain, gene-vocabulary coverage, and possibly preprocessing, so it remains uncertain whether its gap reflects an inherently weaker representation or an untuned or mismatched integration, and whether the ranking holds in multimodal or other-aggregator settings.

selection_reason: 1) Evidence: the best result so far is RNA-only scVI n=200 with multi-profile avgpool (0.650 accuracy, 0.628 F1). With the PCA encoder, adding ResNet50 images through concat fusion gave a modest gain (+0.028 accuracy, +0.038 F1). However, image-only ResNet50 was weak (0.328), so it is unclear whether that gain is real complementary signal or noise, and whether it survives with a stronger RNA representation. 2) This experiment keeps the best RNA-only setup fixed (scVI, multi-profile, avgpool) and adds only the ResNet50 image encoder with concat fusion. It is a clean replication of the image-addition effect on a second RNA backbone. If the gain holds, multimodal fusion is supported. If it shrinks or reverses, images may only help weaker RNA encoders. 3) It is the best use of the budget because it is both exploitation and a clean test.
